sets.title: India's Digital Payment Revolution
sets.context:
Barely a decade ago, cash was the undisputed king of everyday commerce in India, changing hands in markets, buses and tea stalls from dawn to dusk. Today that picture has changed almost beyond recognition. The Unified Payments Interface, launched in 2016, has made instant digital transfers so **ubiquitous** that a roadside vendor selling vegetables is as likely to display a QR code as a large department store. Millions of people who never owned a credit card now move money with a few taps on a mobile phone.

The benefits of this shift have been considerable. Digital payments leave a verifiable trail, which widens the tax base and helps bring informal businesses into the formal economy. For small traders, accepting money electronically removes the risk and inconvenience of handling large amounts of cash. For the government, direct transfer of subsidies and pensions into bank accounts has reduced leakage and ensured that support reaches its intended recipients more reliably than before.

Yet the very convenience that has driven adoption has also opened new avenues for abuse. As transactions have moved online, so too have fraudsters, who use fake payment links, cloned apps and social engineering to deceive the unwary. Rural users and the elderly, often less familiar with the technology, are especially vulnerable. Reports of people losing their savings to a single careless tap have become disturbingly common, and such incidents can **deter** hesitant first-time users from embracing digital tools at all.

Addressing these risks, experts argue, does not mean slowing the momentum of digitisation. Rather, it calls for sustained investment in security, simpler grievance-redress mechanisms and, above all, widespread financial-literacy campaigns. If users are taught to recognise the warning signs of fraud as instinctively as they have learnt to scan a QR code, digital payments can continue to be a force for inclusion rather than a source of anxiety.

sets.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
sets.context:
(A) Within decades, printed books were spreading across Europe, carrying ideas farther and faster than ever before.
(B) For centuries, books had to be copied by hand, a slow and costly process that kept them out of reach of ordinary people.
(C) This changed dramatically in the fifteenth century, when Johannes Gutenberg developed a press that used movable metal type.
(D) His invention allowed identical pages to be produced quickly and in large numbers, drastically lowering the cost of each book.
(E) Today, although much of our reading has moved to screens, the revolution Gutenberg began still shapes how knowledge is shared.
(F) As a result, literacy grew, new thinking flourished, and the foundations of the modern age were laid.

sets.title: Survey on Preferred Mode of Commuting
sets.context: A survey was conducted among 900 people about their preferred mode of commuting: Bus, Metro and Car. 40% of the people preferred the Bus. Of the remaining people, the ratio of those preferring the Metro to those preferring the Car was 5 : 4. Among the Bus users, 25% were women. Among the Metro users, 60% were men. Among the Car users, exactly half were women.

sets.title: Eight Persons in a Single Row
sets.context:

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central idea of the passage?
options: Digital payments in India have completely eliminated the use of cash in all forms of commerce.
Digital payments have brought significant benefits but also new risks of fraud, which must be tackled through security and financial-literacy efforts rather than by slowing digitisation.
The Unified Payments Interface has failed because fraudsters have made digital transactions unsafe for everyone.
Cash remains superior to digital payments and the government should discourage the use of QR codes.
Only large department stores, and not small vendors, have benefited from the shift to digital payments.
questions.explanation: The passage praises the benefits of digital payments, warns of the accompanying fraud risks, and concludes that the answer lies in security, grievance redress and financial literacy, not in slowing digitisation. Option 2 balances both sides and matches the final paragraph. The others overstate one aspect or contradict the text.

source.ref: Modeled on SBI PO Prelims 2024 pattern
